executive_summary: Brazos Bend Coffee Roasters (Tenant) was locked out of Suite 140 at Ridgmar Crossing on August 26, 2025 after withholding August rent to recover an $8,400 rooftop HVAC compressor replacement. The documents show (1) the lease expressly forbids withholding or offsetting rent even if the landlord is in breach; (2) the lease is genuinely ambiguous about who must repair a rooftop HVAC unit that serves only this suite; (3) the landlord's agent demanded a $1,500 'lockout and administrative fee' that appears nowhere in the lease, which Texas Property Code Section 93.012 prohibits and which may take the lockout outside the protection of Section 93.002; and (4) whether the landlord's notice of default was properly 'given' depends on a certified-mail receipt that is not in the file. The most time-sensitive question is whether to seek a writ of reentry in justice court under Section 93.003. Several conclusions are provisional pending the vendor invoice, proof of mailing, and the lease exhibits.

main_issues.title: Was the lockout carried out lawfully?
main_issues.explanation: Texas law allows a commercial landlord to change the locks of a tenant who is behind on rent, but only if it posts a notice saying where a new key can be obtained and provides the key when the tenant pays the delinquent rent. The lease adopts that statute. Tenant's record indicates the key was conditioned on an extra $1,500 fee.
main_issues.customer_position: The extra fee condition took the lockout outside the statute; Tenant may recover possession or terminate and recover damages, the greater of one month's rent or $500, fees and costs.
main_issues.opposing_position: Tenant was delinquent, the lease authorized the lock change, the posted notice was proper, and the fee was a separate matter.
main_issues.current_assessment: Currently favors the customer on the fee condition, but the proof is an email account of a phone call; the reviewer flagged the need for a photograph of the notice and any written key demand.

main_issues.title: Can the landlord charge the $1,500 fee?
main_issues.explanation: Section 93.012 bars charges other than rent or physical damage unless the lease (or an exhibit or amendment) states the amount or how it is computed. The lease in the file lists only a 5% late charge and attorneys' fees.
main_issues.customer_position: The fee is unenforceable and should not be a condition of access.
main_issues.opposing_position: The fee is a recoverable cost or damage item preserved by Section 93.012(b).
main_issues.current_assessment: Favors the customer, subject to review of Exhibits B and C, which are not in the file.

main_issues.title: Who had to repair the rooftop HVAC unit?
main_issues.explanation: The lease defines Building Systems (Landlord's job) to include rooftop HVAC equipment serving the building generally, but separately makes Tenant responsible for HVAC equipment exclusively serving the suite. A rooftop unit dedicated to Suite 140 fits both descriptions.
main_issues.customer_position: Rooftop equipment is a Building System; Landlord warranted the unit at commencement and refused to repair, so Tenant may recover the $8,400.
main_issues.opposing_position: The specific clause on equipment exclusively serving the suite controls; Tenant also never produced the required maintenance contract.
main_issues.current_assessment: Unclear. The skeptical review found both advocates overstated their reading. The vendor invoice and report, and any maintenance records, are needed.

main_issues.title: Was Tenant allowed to withhold August rent?
main_issues.explanation: Two lease clauses say rent may not be withheld or offset for any landlord default, and the self-help clause requires an invoice rather than a deduction.
main_issues.customer_position: The repair was Landlord's duty and the withholding was a reasonable response to its refusal.
main_issues.opposing_position: Offset is flatly prohibited; Tenant's remedy was to invoice Landlord and sue for damages if unpaid.
main_issues.current_assessment: Favors the opposing party. Whether Texas case law ever overrides an express independent-covenant clause is a question for counsel; no such authority is in the local library.

refs.quote: Tenant shall not withhold, abate, or offset Rent on account of any alleged default by Landlord

main_issues.title: Had a lease Event of Default matured before August 26?
main_issues.explanation: The lease requires written notice (by hand, courier, or certified mail; email does not count unless acknowledged in writing) and a ten-day cure before non-payment becomes an Event of Default that triggers lease remedies.
main_issues.customer_position: No certified letter was received; email was not notice; the cure period never started.
main_issues.opposing_position: The letter was mailed certified on August 11; the lease deems notice given three business days after mailing; the cure period expired before the lock change.
main_issues.current_assessment: Unclear and entirely dependent on proof of mailing, which is not in the file. The statutory lock-change right does not depend on these lease mechanics.

time_sensitive_concerns.concern: A sworn complaint for reentry under Property Code Section 93.003 is the statutory route to regain possession quickly; it requires filing in the justice court for the precinct where the premises are located and an oral statement under oath. Delay reduces its practical value and perishable inventory remains inside.
time_sensitive_concerns.date_or_deadline: As soon as possible after the August 26, 2025 lockout; no fixed statutory deadline is stated in the library text

practical_considerations: The amount in dispute for August is $7,717.50 as claimed by Landlord, against Tenant's claimed $8,400 credit; the net difference is small relative to the cost of losing possession, which an attorney may weigh when discussing options.
Tenant's contemporaneous August 26 email is currently the only record of the fee demand; preserving all communications, photographs, and call logs is important.
The guarantor is named personally in the lease; counsel should review the guaranty before any negotiation.
Both sides have attorney's-fee exposure under the lease's prevailing-party clause and Chapter 38 of the Civil Practice and Remedies Code.
questions_for_attorney: Should we file a sworn complaint for reentry under Property Code Section 93.003 now, and what evidence do we need at the hearing?
Does conditioning the new key on a $1,500 fee that is not in the lease make the lockout unlawful under Section 93.002, and what remedies follow under subsection (g)?
Does Section 93.002(h), which lets a lease supersede the statute, change the analysis given that Section 15.2(c) of our lease incorporates Section 93.002?

How would a Texas court likely resolve the conflict between Section 1.10 (Building Systems including rooftop equipment) and Section 7.2 (HVAC exclusively serving the Premises), and what extrinsic evidence would matter?
Given Sections 4.4 and 7.4, was there any lawful way to recover the $8,400 other than invoicing and suing, and how should we present the reimbursement claim now?
If Landlord cannot produce a certified mail receipt, did the ten-day cure period ever start, and who bears the burden of proving mailing under Section 17.1?
Does Tenant's reference to 'the August 11 email attachment' count as a written acknowledgment that converts the email into notice under Section 17.2?
What is the exposure of the personal guarantor, and should we request Exhibit C before negotiating?
Should we tender the undisputed rent now to limit damages and strengthen the reentry request, and how should the tender be worded?
Is there a claim for lost business during the June outage, and what records would support it?
